title: Advent customs
hook: a tree of ornaments telling the story from creation to Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lenten customs: fish in the hall, the Stations at seven, a box on the counter. Your line was lent at home. Did a jar or a box find a place in your house? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

Early December, a bare branch stands in a pot of stones on the dining table. No lights. No tinsel. Each evening after dinner, a child is allowed to hang one homemade ornament on it, and someone reads a short passage from the Bible. A paper apple. A tiny wooden boat. A ram cut out of felt. A ladder made of popsicle sticks. A coat with too many colors. By Christmas the branch is crowded, and anyone who sat at that table has heard a whole story, a few minutes a night, from the garden to the manger. Today's word is the name of that branch.
screen: `A BARE BRANCH IN A POT OF STONES.` → `ONE ORNAMENT A NIGHT.` → `FROM THE GARDEN TO THE MANGER.`

segments.voice: The name comes from a line in Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." Look at what Isaiah sees: an old root, and out of it, something new and green. Christians read that shoot as the Messiah, growing from the family line of David. Next, who Jesse is. Not a king. In the first book of Samuel he's a man of Bethlehem with a house full of sons, and his youngest is out minding the sheep when the prophet comes looking for a king. That youngest boy is David. So the prophecy doesn't say a rod out of the root of David. It reaches back behind the king, to an ordinary household in Bethlehem. Matthew's Gospel names him in its long genealogy at the very start: "And Obed begot Jesse. And Jesse begot David the king." Then, the ornaments. Each one stands for a person or a moment in that family story. A piece of fruit, for Adam and Eve; Genesis never says it was an apple. A boat, for Noah. A ram, for Abraham and Isaac. A ladder, for Jacob's dream. A coat, for Joseph. Families choose their own sets, and no two Jesse trees look quite the same. Last, why it belongs to Advent. Advent waits, and the Jesse tree shows what the waiting was made of: generations of people, some of them flawed, some of them surprising, gathered on one branch as the story that leads to Jesus. It turns the season into a family story read aloud, one name at a time.
screen: `A ROD OUT OF THE ROOT OF JESSE.` · `JESSE, A MAN OF BETHLEHEM.` · `ONE ORNAMENT FOR EACH STORY.` · `A FAMILY TREE, READ ALOUD.` · then, large: `A FLOWER SHALL RISE UP OUT OF HIS ROOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one ornament, at least in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Choose one story from the Bible that you remember: Noah, Ruth, David with his sling, Mary at the door. Ask yourself what small object would stand for it. A boat. A sheaf of wheat. A stone. Hold that image until it's clear. Then, after the bell, if you have paper, scissors or a pen, make it, even badly, and put it somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can read that story again tonight. If you don't, simply let the picture stay with you. The bell holds the time.
Jesse tree. An Advent branch hung with ornaments, one a night, telling the story of Jesus's family line, named for Isaiah's rod out of the root of Jesse. Today's word.

Your line: the family tree. Today, tell someone one story from your own family's past, an ancestor, a move, a hard year survived, and listen for one from theirs. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Some Catholic families, schools and parishes keep a Jesse tree in Advent: a branch or small tree on which an ornament is hung each day, each standing for a figure or story from the Bible, with a short reading.

notes: Isaiah 11:1 is read in Advent (e.g. Tuesday of the first week of Advent, Year A Second Sunday); 'read in Advent' is the only claim made. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of Isaiah 11:1 and Matthew 1:5–6: confirm.
1 Samuel 16 (Douay 1 Kings 16): Jesse the Bethlehemite, David the youngest keeping the sheep, paraphrased. Confirm.

Ornament symbols (apple, boat, ram, ladder, coat) are common examples, presented as choices families make, not a fixed set. The 'apple' for Adam and Eve is a custom; Genesis names no apple. A Keeper may want that said.
